strengths: Addresses a novel and underexplored problem: nonconvex decentralized optimization under heavy-tailed (potentially infinite-variance) gradient noise, with only a p-th moment bound (p in (1,2]), relaxing restrictive prior assumptions of compact domain, strong convexity, and noise symmetry used in the only two prior works on this topic.

Establishes the first decentralized algorithm (GT-NSGDm) that achieves the order-optimal O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)}) rate matching the known centralized lower bound, and a second rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(2p)}) when the tail index p is unknown that is topology-independent for large T and exhibits a speedup factor of n^{1-1/p}.

The negative result (Claim 1) for vanilla normalized decentralized GD is a valuable theoretical contribution that clearly motivates the specific combination of gradient tracking, momentum, and normalization used in the proposed method, and clarifies why naive extensions of centralized techniques fail.

The theoretical analysis is detailed and self-contained, with a full suite of supporting lemmas (consensus error bounds, martingale-based moment bounds, gradient-tracking error decomposition) provided in the appendix, lending credibility to the claimed rates.

Experiments span both controlled synthetic heavy-tailed noise injection (Gaussian, Student's t, Lévy α-stable) on a nonconvex robust regression task and a real-world decentralized Transformer (GPT) training task on Multi30k, across multiple network topologies (ring, directed/undirected exponential, complete), providing reasonably comprehensive empirical validation.

Empirical results support key theoretical claims, including robustness to heavy-tailed noise relative to baselines and speedup with increasing number of nodes n, and the method significantly outperforms baselines in the real Transformer training experiment.
weaknesses: The real-world experimental validation is limited to a very small (3M-parameter) GPT model on a relatively small dataset (Multi30k), which limits confidence that the theoretical/empirical robustness claims extrapolate to realistic large-scale attention model training where heavy-tailed noise is most relevant.

Only in-expectation convergence guarantees are provided; many contemporary works in this area (e.g., several cited baselines in centralized/server settings) provide high-probability bounds, which are arguably more informative under heavy-tailed noise since expectations of heavy-tailed quantities can be dominated by rare large deviations.

The algorithm has three interacting hyperparameters (step size α, momentum β, and implicit dependence on p for the optimal-rate variant), and the momentum schedule for Theorem 1 requires knowledge of p, meaning the fully practical (Theorem 2) variant already sacrifices optimality; the practical trade-off between the two variants could be discussed more thoroughly.

The comparison set of baselines, while reasonable, omits some more recent or stronger decentralized nonlinear methods (e.g., more advanced clipping/sign-based decentralized schemes), and it is unclear how sensitive the reported gains are to the specific (and fairly narrow) hyperparameter grids used for baselines versus GT-NSGDm.

The synthetic dataset designed to mimic token frequency heavy-tailedness is somewhat ad hoc (Bernoulli-based feature construction) and its connection to realistic heavy-tailed gradient noise in language modeling is only loosely justified.

Constants in the derived bounds are not empirically validated or discussed (e.g., no ablation isolating the effect of gradient tracking vs. momentum vs. normalization in the real Transformer experiments), which would strengthen the practical significance of the theoretical improvements over simpler baselines.

strengths: First rigorous derivation of an order-optimal convergence rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)}) for decentralized nonconvex optimization under heavy-tailed noise (only p-th moment, p in (1,2]) that matches the known centralized lower bound, relaxing the restrictive strong-convexity/bounded-domain assumptions of prior decentralized works [29,30].

The negative result (Claim 1) showing that vanilla normalized decentralized GD can be pushed arbitrarily far from the optimum due to heterogeneous local normalization is a nice, clarifying theoretical contribution that motivates the specific combination of gradient tracking + momentum + normalization used in GT-NSGDm.

A second rate is provided for the practically relevant setting where the tail index p is unknown, showing topology-independence and an n^{1-1/p} speedup for p<2, which is a meaningful and non-trivial theoretical result.
The paper provides full, detailed proofs (consensus-error lemmas, martingale-based moment bounds, etc.) rather than only stating results, improving reproducibility of the theory.

Experiments span both a controlled synthetic setting (with injected Gaussian/Student-t/Lévy noise) and a real decentralized Transformer training task, and study dependence on connectivity, noise level, and number of nodes, which aligns with the theoretical claims (e.g., speedup trend in n).
weaknesses: Algorithm parameters (stepsize schedule, momentum coefficient) in Theorem 1 require prior knowledge of T, Δ0, L, λ (and implicitly σ), making the 'optimal' guarantee non-adaptive/impractical without additional knowledge of unknown problem constants; this limitation is not discussed critically in the main text.

The empirical evidence for heavy-tailed noise in the motivating Transformer experiment (Figure 1) is not fully convincing: the noise-norm histograms across epochs look fairly concentrated/bounded compared to the synthetic α-stable reference distribution shown alongside them, which has a visibly longer tail; the claim that noise 'increasingly resembles' α-stable is only qualitative.

The magnitude of the performance gap in the real Transformer experiment (GT-NSGDm reaching near-zero loss while all baselines plateau at loss 5–6) is suspiciously large and raises concerns about whether baselines (especially GT-DSGD and DSGD-Clip, which have theoretical guarantees in other settings) were adequately tuned or implemented correctly; no explanation is given for why standard bounded-variance methods would fail so catastrophically rather than merely converging slower.

Real-world experimental validation is limited in scale and diversity: a single small dataset (Multi30k, ~4.4M tokens), one tiny 3M-parameter GPT model, and only n=8 nodes, which is not strong evidence of general applicability for a top-tier venue; no generalization/test-set evaluation beyond validation loss, and near-zero training/validation loss on a small corpus raises memorization/overfitting concerns rather than demonstrating genuine language-modeling capability.

No variance/error bars are shown for the baseline curves in Figures 2–4 (only GT-NSGDm's variance is highlighted in Fig. 4), making it hard to assess whether the reported gaps are robust across seeds.

The algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: it combines normalization from [27], momentum/error-feedback ideas from [30], and gradient tracking from prior decentralized literature [12]; while the combination and analysis are non-trivial, the individual components are not new.

The convergence bounds in Theorems 1 and 2 contain many additive terms with complex dependence on n, λ, σ, L, Δ0, T, making the practical significance and tightness of the bound difficult to parse without further simplification or numerical illustration of the bound itself (as opposed to just the dominant asymptotic term).

strengths: Establishes the first order-optimal non-asymptotic convergence rate for decentralized nonconvex stochastic optimization under heavy-tailed noise, matching the known centralized lower bound, which is a genuine advance over prior decentralized works (Sun & Chen; Yu et al.) that only handled strongly convex objectives with weaker or unspecified rates.

The negative result (Claim 1) showing vanilla normalized decentralized GD can remain arbitrarily far from the optimum is a nice theoretical contribution that clearly motivates and justifies the specific combination of gradient tracking, momentum-based variance reduction, and normalization used in GT-NSGDm.

Provides two convergence regimes (known and unknown tail index p), with the unknown-p case yielding a topology-independent rate and an interesting n^{1-1/p} speedup, which is a nontrivial and interesting theoretical finding with practical implications for scaling to more nodes under heavy-tailed noise.

Comprehensive and detailed appendix proofs (consensus error bounds, martingale-difference lemmas, gradient tracking analysis) that appear internally consistent and carefully handle the added nonlinearity from normalization.

Experiments span both controlled synthetic heavy-tailed noise injection (Gaussian, Student's-t, Lévy α-stable) and a real-world decentralized Transformer training task across multiple network topologies (ring, directed exponential, complete), giving reasonably convincing empirical support, including corroboration of the theoretical n-speedup and topology-robustness claims.

Related work section carefully and honestly distinguishes the paper's contribution from the two closest prior works, clarifying exactly which restrictive assumptions (compact domain, strong convexity, noise symmetry) are relaxed.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic idea is a fairly natural combination of three already well-established techniques (gradient tracking, momentum-based variance reduction/error-feedback, and gradient normalization), each individually borrowed from prior centralized or decentralized literature; the main novelty is in the analysis and the combination rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic mechanism.

The stated convergence rates require a step size α and momentum parameter β that depend on unknown or hard-to-estimate quantities (Δ0, L, λ, and even p in Theorem 1), which limits practical implementability despite being standard practice in this line of theoretical work.

The convergence guarantees are only in-expectation; no high-probability bounds are provided, unlike several works in the centralized heavy-tailed literature that the paper itself cites (e.g., Sadiev et al., Nguyen et al.) as achieving high-probability optimality.

Empirical comparisons are somewhat narrow: only two truly relevant heavy-tailed decentralized baselines (DSGD-Clip, SClip-EF-Network) are tested, and the real-data Transformer experiments use a very small model (3M parameters) and small network sizes (n=8), which limits the strength of claims about scalability and applicability to large modern models.

The paper does not report wall-clock/communication overhead comparisons versus baselines, which would be relevant since gradient tracking doubles the communicated quantities per round relative to plain DSGD-type methods.

The dependence of the bound on λ, n, and p in Theorem 1's full (non-asymptotic) expression is fairly complex with many additive terms, and the paper's discussion focuses mainly on the asymptotically dominant terms, leaving the practical regime where these bounds are tight or informative somewhat unclear.

strengths: Provides the first decentralized algorithm (GT-NSGDm) achieving an order-optimal non-asymptotic convergence rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)}) for general nonconvex, L-smooth functions under heavy-tailed noise with only a p-th moment bound, matching the centralized lower bound, without requiring strong convexity or bounded-gradient/compact-domain assumptions as in prior decentralized works [29,30].

Also derives a rate for the unknown-p case that matches the best centralized rate, is topology-independent in the dominant regime, and exhibits a speedup factor n^{1-1/p} in the number of nodes, which is a nontrivial and interesting finding.

Includes an insightful negative result (Claim 1) showing that vanilla normalized decentralized gradient descent (without gradient tracking/momentum) can be made arbitrarily far from optimal, which clearly motivates the algorithmic design choices and adds conceptual value beyond just presenting a new method.

The theoretical analysis is detailed and appears carefully constructed, with a clear proof roadmap (consensus error bounds, gradient estimation error decomposition, and final rate derivation) provided in the appendix.

Experiments span both a controlled synthetic setting (mimicking heavy-tailed token/gradient noise) and a decentralized Transformer training task, with multiple graph topologies, extensive baseline comparisons (8 baselines), and reported hyperparameter search grids, aiding reproducibility.
Careful comparative discussion of parameter dependencies against related centralized/decentralized rates (Remarks 5-8) shows attention to the practical implications and limitations of the bounds.
weaknesses: The convergence bounds contain many additive terms with intricate dependencies on n, λ, p, and the practical benefit (e.g., the claimed speedup or topology independence) only manifests in specific asymptotic/high-noise regimes for large T, which may limit the practical relevance of the headline claims.

The real-world Transformer experiment is very small scale (3M parameters, 8 nodes, Multi30k dataset), which limits confidence that the theoretical advantages translate to more realistic large-scale decentralized training scenarios (e.g., larger models, more nodes, real heterogeneous data splits).

In Table 1, GT-NSGDm's practical advantage over the only other theoretically-grounded heavy-tailed baseline (SClip-EF-Network) is large, but it only nearly matches (does not exceed) a heuristic baseline (DSGD-GClip) that has no theoretical guarantees, somewhat weakening the practical case for the added algorithmic/theoretical complexity.

Only in-expectation convergence guarantees are given; no high-probability bounds are provided, which is often more informative under heavy-tailed noise since expectations can be dominated by rare large deviations.

The synthetic experiment's noise injection and network sizes are relatively small (n=20, 1k samples), and it is unclear how sensitive the empirical speedup findings (Fig. 3c) are to noise level or problem dimension choices beyond the tested range.

The algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental in that it combines known building blocks (gradient tracking, momentum-based variance reduction, gradient normalization) from existing centralized/decentralized literature; the primary novel technical contribution is the careful joint analysis handling the interaction of nonlinearity (normalization) with gradient tracking and momentum under heavy tails.

strengths: Establishes, for the first time in the decentralized setting, an order-optimal convergence rate O(1/T^{(p-1)/(3p-2)}) for nonconvex smooth objectives under heavy-tailed noise with only p-th moment bounds, matching the centralized lower bound, and also provides a p-agnostic rate matching the best centralized result.
Relaxes restrictive assumptions of prior decentralized heavy-tailed-noise works (strong convexity, bounded domain/gradients, noise symmetry), broadening applicability.

The negative result (Claim 1) that vanilla normalized decentralized GD can remain arbitrarily far from the optimum is a nice, clarifying motivation for why gradient tracking and momentum are needed together with normalization.

The theoretical analysis is detailed and self-contained, with a clear proof roadmap (consensus error lemmas, gradient estimation error decomposition) and explicit non-asymptotic bounds with all problem constants retained.

Experiments span multiple heavy-tailed noise types (Student's t, Lévy α-stable), multiple graph topologies (ring, directed/undirected exponential, complete), and both synthetic regression and a real Transformer/language-modeling task, giving reasonably broad empirical coverage.
weaknesses: In the Transformer experiment, the two baselines with theoretical guarantees under heavy-tailed noise (DSGD-Clip, SClip-EF-Network) essentially fail to train (loss ~5.6, near initialization), which looks like a tuning/implementation issue rather than a genuine limitation of those methods, undermining confidence in the fairness of the comparison; meanwhile GT-NSGDm's performance is only marginally better than the untheorized heuristic DSGD-GClip baseline, weakening the practical case for the proposed method.

The claimed node-speedup (factor n^{1-1/p}) is not cleanly supported empirically: Figure 3(c) shows final error increasing from n=20 to n=40 (0.20 -> 0.21), contradicting the monotonic speedup narrative, and this discrepancy is not discussed or explained.

The Transformer experiment is very small-scale (3M parameters, ~4.4M tokens, 8 simulated nodes on a single GPU), limiting the strength of evidence for practical relevance to real large-scale distributed training under heavy-tailed noise.

The algorithmic contribution is largely a combination of existing components (normalization+momentum from centralized heavy-tailed literature, standard gradient tracking); the main novelty is the coupled analysis, which, while technically demanding, is an incremental extension rather than a conceptually new algorithmic idea.

Only in-expectation guarantees are provided, whereas much recent heavy-tailed-noise literature (including several cited works) emphasizes high-probability bounds, which are generally more informative under heavy-tailed/unbounded-variance regimes.

Practical hyperparameter selection (α, β) requires prior knowledge of T, ∆0, L, λ, n, which is a nontrivial burden; while Remark 7 partially addresses the λ dependence, the need to fix the horizon T in advance for the stated rates is not clearly acknowledged as a limitation.
Synthetic experiments lack reported variance/confidence intervals across runs (unlike the Transformer table), making it hard to assess robustness of the reported curves and speedup claims.

strengths: The paper closes an important theoretical gap by providing the first order-optimal convergence rate (matching the centralized lower bound) for decentralized nonconvex stochastic optimization under heavy-tailed noise with only p-th moment bounds, p in (1,2].

The algorithmic design is well-motivated: Claim 1 and Remark 3 give a clean, illustrative negative result showing that vanilla decentralized normalized SGD fails due to heterogeneous local gradient norms, clearly justifying the need for gradient tracking combined with normalization and momentum.

Two convergence results are provided (known and unknown tail index p), and the unknown-p case yields a topology-independent rate with a favorable n^(1-1/p) speedup, which is a nontrivial and interesting finding.

The theoretical analysis is thorough and self-contained, with a clear proof roadmap and a sequence of well-organized lemmas (consensus error bounds, martingale difference bounds via Lemma 5, average/stacked gradient estimation error bounds) that carefully handle the nonlinearity introduced by normalization.

Experiments span both controlled synthetic heavy-tailed noise injection (Gaussian, Student's-t, Lévy alpha-stable) and a more realistic decentralized Transformer training task, across multiple network topologies (ring, directed/undirected exponential, complete), which supports the practical relevance of the theory.

Empirical studies specifically probing dependence on λ, σ, and n (Figure 3) are a nice touch that directly connects back to the theoretical remarks (Remarks 5, 6, 8), improving the paper's internal consistency.

The related work section is detailed and carefully differentiates the paper's contribution from prior decentralized heavy-tailed-noise works (e.g., [29], [30]), correctly identifying their strong-convexity/bounded-domain limitations.
weaknesses: The real-world Transformer experiment uses a small model (3M parameters) and small dataset (Multi30k), and the authors themselves note the decentralized training experiment is 'simulated' with 'practical limitations,' which somewhat limits the empirical significance of the results for large-scale, realistic decentralized/federated settings.

In Table 1, GT-NSGDm is outperformed by DSGD-GClip (a baseline without theoretical guarantees under heavy-tailed noise) on all three topologies, so the practical empirical advantage of the proposed method over simple heuristics is not fully established; the paper's claim of being 'more robust and efficient' is only relative to the theoretically-guaranteed baselines.

The known-p algorithm's step size (5) depends on network parameters n and λ, which may be difficult to obtain a priori in fully decentralized systems without extra coordination; while Remark 7 partially addresses this, the fix (estimating λ via a specific Laplacian-based W) is somewhat limited in applicability to general graphs.

The theoretical results are in-expectation only; no high-probability bounds are provided, unlike some recent centralized heavy-tailed works (e.g., [24, 36, 37, 44]), which would strengthen the practical relevance of the guarantees.

The experimental section, while broad, uses relatively small n (up to 40 for synthetic and only 8 for Transformer experiments) making it hard to fully validate the asymptotic n^(1-1/p) speedup claim at larger scale.

The paper's dense/heavy theoretical exposition (many nested lemmas, several free parameters in the bounds) could benefit from more intuition or a summarized proof sketch in the main text to aid readability, though this is somewhat mitigated by the 'Proof structure' paragraph.
